e-10013.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation Given a Corresponding Perfect Square
e-10013.problem:
Solve the equation $x^2 -10x = -24.$ 

*Hint: Use the fact that $x^2 -10x +25$ is a perfect square.*
e-10013.worked_solution:
Using the hint, we have

$$
x^2 -10x +25 = (x-5)^2.
$$

First, we complete the square on the left-hand side: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-10x & =-24 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 5\cdot x & =-24 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 5\cdot x+{5}^{2}-{5}^{2} & =-24 \\ (x-5{)}^{2}-25 & =-24\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we isolate the perfect square by adding $25$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-5{)}^{2}-25+25 & =-24+25 \\ (x-5{)}^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

We now solve the equation using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-5{)}^{2} & =1 \\ \sqrt{(x-5{)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{1} \\ |x-5| & =1 \\ x-5 & =\pm 1 \\ x & =5\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =5-1=4 \\ {x}_{2} & =5+1=6\end{aligned}
$$

e-1431.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation When the Solutions Are Rational
e-1431.problem: Write the equation $x^2 + 6x +5= 0$ in the form $(x+p)^2=q,$ and hence solve the equation.
e-1431.worked_solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+6x+5 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+6x & =-5 \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 3\cdot x & =-5 \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 3\cdot x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2} & =-5 \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3\cdot x+{3}^{2})-9 & =-5 \\ (x+3{)}^{2}-9 & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3{)}^{2}-9 & =-5 \\ (x+3{)}^{2} & =-5+9 \\ (x+3{)}^{2} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, $p=3$ and $q=4.$ Now, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3{)}^{2} & =4 \\ \sqrt{(x+3{)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{4} \\ |x+3| & =2 \\ x+3 & =\pm 2 \\ x & =-3\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-3+2=-1 \\ {x}_{2} & =-3-2=-5\end{aligned}
$$

e-1432.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation When the Solutions Are Irrational
e-1432.worked_solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2x-1 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2x & =1 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 1\cdot x & =1 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 1\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2} & =1 \\ ({x}^{2}-2x+1)-1 & =1 \\ (x-1{)}^{2}-1 & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square and solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-1{)}^{2}-1 & =1 \\ (x-1{)}^{2} & =2 \\ \sqrt{(x-1{)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{2} \\ |x-1| & =\sqrt{2} \\ x-1 & =\pm \sqrt{2} \\ x & =1\pm \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our solutions are

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =1+\sqrt{2}, \\ {x}_{2} & =1-\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

e
 p+q=3,x=−6 and x=1
Submit

EXPLANATION

Then, we isolate the perfect square and solve the equation using the square-root method: (x+3)2−9=−8(x+3)2=1

So, p=3,q=1, and p+q=4.

Next, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

(x+3)2=1(x+3)2=1x+3=±1x=−3±1

We simplify the two solutions: x=−3+1=−2x=−3−1=−4

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation When the Solutions Are Rational
content.problem: The equation ${x}^{2}+6x+8=0$ can be written in the form $(x+p{)}^{2}=q.$ Find $\,p+q,$ and solve the equation.
content.worked_solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+6x+8 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+6x & =-8 \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 3\cdot x & =-8 \\ {x}^{2}+2\cdot 3\cdot x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2} & =-8 \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot 3\cdot x+{3}^{2})-9 & =-8 \\ (x+3{)}^{2}-9 & =-8\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square and solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3{)}^{2}-9 & =-8 \\ (x+3{)}^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=3,q=1,$ and $p+q=4.$

Next, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3{)}^{2} & =1 \\ \sqrt{(x+3{)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{1} \\ x+3 & =\pm 1 \\ x & =-3\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-3+1=-2 \\ x & =-3-1=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-4$ and $x=-2.$

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: The equation ${a}^{2}+8a=48$ can be written in the form $(a+p{)}^{2}=q.$ Find $p+q,$ and solve the equation.
after.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+8a & =48 \\ {a}^{2}+2\cdot 4\cdot a & =48 \\ {a}^{2}+2\cdot 4\cdot a+{4}^{2}-{4}^{2} & =48 \\ ({a}^{2}+2\cdot 4\cdot a+{4}^{2})-16 & =48 \\ {(a+4)}^{2}-16 & =48\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(a+4{)}^{2}-16 & =48 \\ (a+4{)}^{2} & =64\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=4,q=64,$ and $p+q=68.$

Next, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(a+4{)}^{2} & =64 \\ \sqrt{(a+4{)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{64} \\ a+4 & =\pm 8 \\ a & =-4\pm 8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $a=-12$ and $a=4.$

(a+4)2=64(a+4)2=64a+4=±8a=−4±8

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation When the Solutions Are Rational
content.problem: The equation ${a}^{2}+8a=48$ can be written in the form $(a+p{)}^{2}=q.$ Find $p+q,$ and solve the equation.
content.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+8a & =48 \\ {a}^{2}+2\cdot 4\cdot a & =48 \\ {a}^{2}+2\cdot 4\cdot a+{4}^{2}-{4}^{2} & =48 \\ ({a}^{2}+2\cdot 4\cdot a+{4}^{2})-16 & =48 \\ {(a+4)}^{2}-16 & =48\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(a+4{)}^{2}-16 & =48 \\ (a+4{)}^{2} & =64\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=4,q=64,$ and $p+q=68.$

Next, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(a+4{)}^{2} & =64 \\ \sqrt{(a+4{)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{64} \\ a+4 & =\pm 8 \\ a & =-4\pm 8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $a=-12$ and $a=4.$

after.problem: The equation ${a}^{2}+8a=9$ can be written in the form $(a+p{)}^{2}=q.$ Find $\,p+q,$ and solve the equation.
after.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+8a & =9 \\ {a}^{2}+2\cdot a\cdot 4 & =9 \\ {a}^{2}+2\cdot a\cdot 4+{4}^{2}-{4}^{2} & =9 \\ ({a}^{2}+2\cdot a\cdot 4+{4}^{2})-{4}^{2} & =9 \\ ({a}^{2}+2\cdot a\cdot 4+{4}^{2})-16 & =9 \\ (a+4{)}^{2}-16 & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(a+4{)}^{2}-16 & =9 \\ (a+4{)}^{2} & =25\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=4,q=25,$ and $p+q=29.$

Now, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(a+4{)}^{2} & =25 \\ \sqrt{(a+4{)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{25} \\ a+4 & =\pm 5 \\ a & =-4\pm 5\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =-4+5=1 \\ {a}_{2} & =-4-5=-9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $a=1$ and $a=-9.$

EXPLANATION

Then, we isolate the perfect square: (a+4)2−16=9(a+4)2=25

So, p=4,q=25, and p+q=29.

Now, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

(a+4)2=25(a+4)2=25a+4=±5a=−4±5 We simplify the two solutions: a1=−4+5=1a2=−4−5=−9

Therefore, the solutions are a=1 and a=−9.

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Quadratic Equation When the Solutions Are Rational
content.problem: The equation ${a}^{2}+8a=9$ can be written in the form $(a+p{)}^{2}=q.$ Find $\,p+q,$ and solve the equation.
content.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+8a & =9 \\ {a}^{2}+2\cdot a\cdot 4 & =9 \\ {a}^{2}+2\cdot a\cdot 4+{4}^{2}-{4}^{2} & =9 \\ ({a}^{2}+2\cdot a\cdot 4+{4}^{2})-{4}^{2} & =9 \\ ({a}^{2}+2\cdot a\cdot 4+{4}^{2})-16 & =9 \\ (a+4{)}^{2}-16 & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(a+4{)}^{2}-16 & =9 \\ (a+4{)}^{2} & =25\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=4,q=25,$ and $p+q=29.$

Now, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(a+4{)}^{2} & =25 \\ \sqrt{(a+4{)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{25} \\ a+4 & =\pm 5 \\ a & =-4\pm 5\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & =-4+5=1 \\ {a}_{2} & =-4-5=-9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $a=1$ and $a=-9.$

The equation x2−20x−21=0 can be written in the form (x+p)2=q. Find p+q, and solve the equation.

a
p+q=100,x=−11 and x=−1
b
p+q=111,x=−1 and x=21
c
p+q=121,x=−1 and x=21
d
p+q=101,x=1 and x=11
e
p+q=111,x=−11 and x=1
Submit

decision.explanation: Completing the square gives (x-10)^2=121, so p=-10 and q=121, yielding p+q=111. Then x=10±11, giving x=-1 and x=21.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: The equation ${x}^{2}-20x-21=0$ can be written in the form $(x+p{)}^{2}=q.$ Find $\,p+q,$ and solve the equation.
after.worked_solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-20x-21 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-20x & =21 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 10\cdot x & =21 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 10\cdot x+{10}^{2}-{10}^{2} & =21 \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 10\cdot x+{10}^{2})-100 & =21 \\ (x-10{)}^{2}-100 & =21\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-10{)}^{2}-100 & =21 \\ (x-10{)}^{2} & =121\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=-10,q=121,$ and $p+q=111.$

Now, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-10{)}^{2} & =121 \\ \sqrt{(x-10{)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{121} \\ x-10 & =\pm 11 \\ x & =10\pm 11\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =10+11=21 \\ x & =10-11=-1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x=-1$ and $x=21.$

Question 10

The equation x2−20x−21=0 can be written in the form (x+p)2=q. Find p+q, and solve the equation.

a
p+q=100,x=−11 and x=−1
b
p+q=111,x=−1 and x=21
c
p+q=121,x=−1 and x=21
d
p+q=101,x=1 and x=11
e
p+q=111,x=−11 and x=1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side: x2−20x−21=0x2−20x=21x2−2⋅10⋅x=21x2−2⋅10⋅x+102−102=21(x2−2⋅10⋅x+102)−100=21(x−10)2−100=21

Then, we isolate the perfect square: (x−10)2−100=21(x−10)2=121

So, p=−10,q=121, and p+q=111.

Now, we solve the equation using the square-root method: (x−10)2=121(x−10)2=121x−10=±11x=10±11

We simplify the two solutions: x=10+11=21x=10−11=−1

So, the solutions are x=−1 and x=21.

content.problem: The equation ${x}^{2}-20x-21=0$ can be written in the form $(x+p{)}^{2}=q.$ Find $\,p+q,$ and solve the equation.
content.worked_solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-20x-21 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-20x & =21 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 10\cdot x & =21 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 10\cdot x+{10}^{2}-{10}^{2} & =21 \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 10\cdot x+{10}^{2})-100 & =21 \\ (x-10{)}^{2}-100 & =21\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-10{)}^{2}-100 & =21 \\ (x-10{)}^{2} & =121\end{aligned}
$$

So, $p=-10,q=121,$ and $p+q=111.$

Now, we solve the equation using the square-root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-10{)}^{2} & =121 \\ \sqrt{(x-10{)}^{2}} & =\sqrt{121} \\ x-10 & =\pm 11 \\ x & =10\pm 11\end{aligned}
$$

We simplify the two solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =10+11=21 \\ x & =10-11=-1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solutions are $x=-1$ and $x=21.$

$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+2{)}^{2}-4 & =9 \\ (y+2{)}^{2} & =13\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $p=2,$ $q=13,$ and $p+q=15.$

EXPLANATION

First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side: y2+4y−9=0y2+4y=9y2+2⋅2⋅y=9y2+2⋅2⋅y+22−22=9(y+2)2−4=9

Then, we isolate the perfect square: (y+2)2−4=9(y+2)2=13

Hence, p=2, q=13, and p+q=15.

content.problem: The equation ${y}^{2}+4y-9=0$ can be written in the form $(y+p{)}^{2}=q.$   Find $p+q.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we move the constant term to the right-hand side and complete the square on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+4y-9 & =0 \\ {y}^{2}+4y & =9 \\ {y}^{2}+2\cdot 2\cdot y & =9 \\ {y}^{2}+2\cdot 2\cdot y+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2} & =9 \\ (y+2{)}^{2}-4 & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we isolate the perfect square:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+2{)}^{2}-4 & =9 \\ (y+2{)}^{2} & =13\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $p=2,$ $q=13,$ and $p+q=15.$
